title: Mirabel and the Glasshouse
premise: Wren Vane has spent three years mailing unsent confessions to the Glasshouse, the orchard cottage that burned the night his sister Mirabel disappeared, writing postcards he never signs. When the Vane family estate is scheduled for auction and demolition, Wren returns home, where his aunts, uncles, and estranged mother have each arranged their lives around a different version of what happened to Mirabel. As the auction date approaches, old letters surface in the walls of the surviving greenhouse, forcing each family member to choose between the loyalty that held them together and the truth that could shatter them. In the end, Wren learns Mirabel left voluntarily and asked him, years ago, to keep her secret — and by finally saying it aloud at the auction itself, he frees both the family and himself, keeping only the Glasshouse's foundation stone as the family begins, tentatively, to rebuild.
about_author: Coral Winterbourne is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing other people's unsent letters before turning to fiction. She writes about quiet families, coastal towns, and the things we almost say, and lives within sight of an abandoned greenhouse.

chapters.title: Postcards to Ash
chapters.summary: Wren, in his city flat, writes another unsigned postcard to the burned Glasshouse address, revealing his three-year ritual of almost-confession. A solicitor's letter arrives: the Vane estate goes to auction in six weeks. POV: Wren. Emotional beat: dread disguised as routine; the past has found a deadline.

chapters.title: The Family Arrangement
chapters.summary: Wren travels to the coastal town and observes how each relative orbits the family myth: Aunt Ivy tends the surviving greenhouse, Uncle Bram drinks to Mirabel's memory, his mother Odile refuses to say her daughter's name. POV: Wren. Emotional beat: the eerie choreography of a household built around an absence.

chapters.title: What the Greenhouse Kept
chapters.summary: Ivy gives Wren a key to the glasshouse, the only structure spared by the fire, and asks him — too casually — why he really came back. He lies. Inside, he finds fresh flowers on Mirabel's old potting bench. Someone still visits. POV: Wren. Emotional beat: suspicion blooming like heat under glass.

chapters.title: Odile's Version
chapters.summary: In Odile's immaculate house, Wren hears the official story: Mirabel ran off with a traveling musician, wrote once, never again. His mother's grief is polished, rehearsed, and slightly wrong in its details. POV: Wren. Emotional beat: love curdled into curation; he recognizes his own habit of editing truth.

chapters.title: Bram at the Anchor Inn
chapters.summary: Drunk Uncle Bram tells a second version: he saw Mirabel that night, walking toward the cliffs, and said nothing because she begged him to. He's carried the loyalty like a stone ever since. POV: Wren. Emotional beat: the first crack — someone else knows something, and it cost him decades.

chapters.title: The Auction Catalogue
chapters.summary: The auctioneer's catalogue arrives; lot forty-one is 'contents of the glasshouse, unexamined.' Wren realizes strangers will handle Mirabel's things, will walk the ground where the story lives. He considers buying everything just to bury it again. POV: Wren. Emotional beat: possessive panic; silence feels like protection until it doesn't.

chapters.title: Ivy's Letters
chapters.summary: Renovating a collapsed shelf, Wren discovers letters hidden in the greenhouse wall — Mirabel's handwriting, addressed to him, dated after the fire. He reads one and stops cold: she was alive, and she chose not to be found. POV: Wren. Emotional beat: vertigo; the ground of his grief shifts beneath him.

chapters.title: The Question Takes Shape
chapters.summary: Wren confronts Ivy, who admits she knew Mirabel lived and helped hide her, believing the family would break without its shared sorrow. 'We arranged ourselves around the loss,' Ivy says. 'Take it away and what are we?' POV: alternating Wren and Ivy. Emotional beat: loyalty and truth revealed as rival architects of the same house.

chapters.title: Mirabel, Somewhere South
chapters.summary: A flashback chapter in Mirabel's voice: the night of the fire, her escape, her first year alone, her letters to Wren that Ivy intercepted and hid — to protect Wren from choosing between sister and mother. POV: Mirabel. Emotional beat: tenderness and fury; love practiced through absence.

chapters.title: Odile Suspects
chapters.summary: Odile notices the disturbed shelf and the missing letters; her composure fractures for the first time in years. She accuses Ivy of theft, of cruelty, of keeping Mirabel from her. The family's polite architecture groans. POV: Wren observing. Emotional beat: the myth defending itself through the person who built it.

chapters.title: Lot Forty-One
chapters.summary: At a preview event, Wren watches strangers appraise the glasshouse contents and overhears a buyer call Mirabel's things 'charming period ephemera.' Something in him hardens: these are not objects, they're evidence of a life. POV: Wren. Emotional beat: grief converting into resolve.

chapters.title: The Second Letter
chapters.summary: Wren reads Mirabel's second hidden letter: she explains why she left — a truth about their father, long dead, that Odile buried even deeper than the fire. She asked Wren to decide, someday, whether the family could survive knowing. POV: Wren. Emotional beat: inheritance of an unbearable choice.

chapters.title: What Father Did
chapters.summary: Piecing together the father's secret — financial ruin, a forged will, and the fire's true origin as insurance — Wren understands why Mirabel fled rather than live inside the lie. The family's loyalty was never to each other; it was to the cover story. POV: Wren. Emotional beat: the sick clarity of seeing the whole machine at once.

chapters.title: Bram Comes Clean
chapters.summary: Wren shows Bram the letters. Bram confesses fully: he helped Mirabel reach the bus station that night and has drunk to keep the secret quiet. Relieved and terrified, he agrees the truth must come out before demolition. POV: Wren. Emotional beat: two men setting down stones they've carried for years.

chapters.title: Odile Alone
chapters.summary: A quiet interlude in Odile's POV: her memories of the marriage, the forgery, the night she chose the lie over her daughters. She is not a villain but a woman who mistook control for survival. POV: Odile. Emotional beat: tragic sympathy; the reader sees how the arrangement began.

chapters.title: The Confrontation in the Glasshouse
chapters.summary: Wren gathers Ivy, Bram, and Odile among the glass panes and lays out the letters. Odile denies, then rages, then breaks: she knew Mirabel was alive all along. The family's central fiction collapses in a single evening. POV: Wren. Emotional beat: the climax's first detonation — truth spoken, nothing spared.

chapters.title: Where Is She Now
chapters.summary: Under pressure, Ivy reveals Mirabel's last known address, sent yearly and never answered. Wren must decide whether to find her or honor her wish to stay gone — while the auction looms in nine days. POV: Wren. Emotional beat: the question sharpened to a point: which loyalty is real?

chapters.title: The Road South
chapters.summary: Wren drives to the coastal town where Mirabel lives under another name, runs a small nursery, and has a life. He watches her from across the street for a day, drafting and discarding a dozen openings. POV: Wren. Emotional beat: terror of the actual conversation after years of practicing the almost-said.

chapters.title: Saying It
chapters.summary: Wren finally speaks to Mirabel. She isn't angry; she's been waiting to see if he'd come. They talk through the night — the fire, the father, the letters, the family she loved enough to leave. She agrees to come back, on one condition: no more arrangements. POV: alternating Wren and Mirabel. Emotional beat: catharsis; the almost-said finally said.

chapters.title: The Auction
chapters.summary: Auction day. As lot forty-one is called, Mirabel walks into the marquee. The room stops. Odile stands. Wren, holding the microphone meant for bidding, tells the assembled town the true story instead — then withdraws the lot. POV: Wren. Emotional beat: public climax; private truth offered up as the only honest bid.

chapters.title: Demolition Day
chapters.summary: The burnt cottage comes down as planned, but the family watches together, changed: Odile and Mirabel speak haltingly, Ivy stops tending a grave that was never there, Bram pours out his last bottle. What they demolish is the arrangement, not each other. POV: rotating family members. Emotional beat: mourning completed at last.

chapters.title: The Foundation Stone
chapters.summary: Epilogue, one year later: the family keeps the glasshouse, restored, with Mirabel's nursery business inside. Wren mails one final postcard — signed this time — to an address that now exists again. Some questions were never meant to be answered quietly. POV: Wren. Emotional beat: resolution; truth, once spoken, becomes the new thing the family arranges itself around — willingly.
